I recently read @paulg's essay, “How to Do Great Work”, and one idea has been stuck in my head ever since.

Most of us spend a lot of time worrying about whether we're working hard enough. We look at successful people and assume they got there because they had more discipline, better habits, or a clearer plan than everyone else.

But Paul argues that great work often starts somewhere much simpler: curiosity. 

The people who end up doing exceptional things are usually the ones who become deeply interested in something and keep following that interest further than most people are willing to go.

The more I thought about it, the more it made sense.

If you're genuinely curious about something, you don't need to be constantly motivated to learn about it. 

You naturally spend more time on it. You ask more questions. You notice details others overlook. You keep going even when progress feels slow because the process itself is rewarding.

That creates a huge advantage over time.

Two people can start at the same level today. One treats learning as an obligation. The other is pulled forward by genuine curiosity. After a few weeks, the difference is small. After a few years, it can be enormous.

What I found most interesting is that Paul doesn't suggest starting with a detailed roadmap for success. 

Instead, he suggests paying attention to what you're unusually curious about—the topics, problems, or ideas that keep pulling your attention back. 

Those interests might seem insignificant at first, but they often contain clues about where you'll do your best work.

My biggest takeaway from the essay is that curiosity isn't a distraction from meaningful work. It's often the starting point. 

The things you keep coming back to, the questions you can't stop thinking about, and the subjects you enjoy exploring when nobody is asking you to—those may be more important than any career plan you could write down.

Sometimes great work isn't about finding the right path.

It's about paying attention to what keeps pulling you down it.

Source: Paul Graham, How to Do Great Work
